why: The stem quotes, almost word for word, the chapter's own **Remember** box on its opening page: "The branch of chemistry which deals with the study of seperation, identification, qualitative and quantitative determination of the compositions of different substances, is called **analytical chemistry**." Each of the other three names a branch defined by the KIND of matter or the KIND of change it studies, not by the act of measuring composition: physical chemistry studies the physical behaviour and energetics of matter, inorganic chemistry the compounds of the elements other than the hydrocarbons, and organic chemistry the compounds of carbon. Separation, identification and quantitative determination is the definition of analytical chemistry.

A quantitative property is one that can be assigned a NUMBER by measurement against a unit. Mass is measured in kilograms, length in metres and volume in cubic metres, so all three carry a magnitude and a unit and can be compared numerically. **Colour** is a qualitative property: the chapter lists it under qualitative identification — "Identification may be based on differences in colour, odour, melting point, boiling point, and reactivity" — where it serves to tell substances apart, not to measure how much of one is present. It is the odd one out because it has no unit and no magnitude.

The SI base unit of mass is the **kilogram**. The other three fail for different reasons and each failure is worth naming: the mole is an SI base unit but of AMOUNT OF SUBSTANCE, not of mass; the pound is a unit of mass but belongs to the imperial system, not to SI; and \(\mathrm{m^3}\) is the SI unit of VOLUME. Note that mass is the one SI base unit whose name already carries a prefix, so "kilogram" and not "gram" is the correct answer.

By the chapter's rule 5, in a number written in scientific notation ALL the digits of the coefficient are significant; the power of ten only fixes the position of the decimal point and contributes nothing. The coefficient of \(1.50 \times 10^4\) is 1.50, whose digits are 1, 5 and 0 — and the terminal zero counts here because it stands to the right of the decimal point (rule 4), so the value is **3**. Two would be the count only if the zero were dropped, four and six would require digits the number does not have; in particular 4 is the trap of counting the exponent's digits as well.

Again by rule 5, every digit of the coefficient in scientific notation is significant. The coefficient of \(6.022 \times 10^{23}\ \mathrm{mol^{-1}}\) is 6.022, whose digits are 6, 0, 2 and 2 — and the internal zero is significant by rule 2 (a zero between two non-zero digits always counts) — giving **4**. Three would mean discarding that internal zero, which rule 2 forbids; five and six would need the exponent 23 to contribute digits, which it never does.

The decomposition is \(\mathrm{CaCO_3} \xrightarrow{\ \Delta\ } \mathrm{CaO} + \mathrm{CO_2}\). Formula masses: \(\mathrm{CaCO_3} = 40 + 12 + 3 \times 16 = 100\) and \(\mathrm{CaO} = 40 + 16 = 56\), so 100 g of the carbonate gives 56 g of the oxide. Hence 25 g gives \(\dfrac{56}{100} \times 25 = \mathbf{14.0\ g}\). Of the distractors only one has a traceable origin: 2.8 g is what 5 g of \(\mathrm{CaCO_3}\) would give, which is the chapter's own worked Problem 2.12 — so it is the answer to a neighbouring question, not to this one. 8.4 g and 28.0 g follow from no consistent reading of the data; 28.0 g is simply twice the correct value.

Complete combustion of methane is \(\mathrm{CH_4} + 2\,\mathrm{O_2} \longrightarrow \mathrm{CO_2} + 2\,\mathrm{H_2O}\). One mole of \(\mathrm{CH_4}\) (16 g) gives two moles of water (36 g), so 12 g of methane gives \(\dfrac{12}{16} \times 36 = \mathbf{27\ g}\) of water. 36 g is the trap of quoting the water formed from a FULL 16 g of methane rather than from the 12 g given; 16 is the molar mass of methane itself; 56 corresponds to no quantity in this reaction.

Take 100 g of the compound: 75.8 g of A and 24.2 g of B. Moles are \(75.8/75 = 1.011\) and \(24.2/16 = 1.513\), and dividing by the smaller gives A : B \(= 1 : 1.497\), i.e. \(2 : 3\), so the formula is \(\mathbf{A_2B_3}\). Testing the alternatives directly settles it: the mass percentage of A works out at 82.4 % for AB, 90.4 % for \(\mathrm{A_2B}\) and 70.1 % for \(\mathrm{AB_2}\), against the 75.8 % the question states — and \(\mathrm{A_2B_3}\) returns 75.76 %, which rounds exactly to the printed figure.

In 100 g of the hydrocarbon there are 79.87 g of carbon and 20.13 g of hydrogen, giving \(79.87/12 = 6.656\) mol C and \(20.13/1.008 = 19.97\) mol H. Dividing by the smaller, H : C \(= 3.00 : 1\), so the empirical formula is \(\mathbf{CH_3}\). Working the other way confirms it and rules the rest out: the carbon percentage is 92.3 % for CH, 85.6 % for \(\mathrm{CH_2}\) and 82.6 % for \(\mathrm{C_2H_5}\), while \(\mathrm{CH_3}\) gives 79.87 % C and 20.13 % H — the question's own two figures, to the digit.

Aluminium burns as \(4\,\mathrm{Al} + 3\,\mathrm{O_2} \longrightarrow 2\,\mathrm{Al_2O_3}\). With At. mass Al = 27, the 27 g given is exactly 1 mol of Al, which by the equation needs \(\tfrac{3}{4}\) mol of \(\mathrm{O_2}\); at \(32\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\) that is \(0.75 \times 32 = \mathbf{24\ g}\). The distractors are the familiar wrong mole ratios: 32 g assumes 1 mol of \(\mathrm{O_2}\) (a 1:1 ratio), 16 g assumes half a mole, and 8 g corresponds to a quarter — none of which balances the equation.

The molar mass of \(\mathrm{CuSO_4 \cdot 5H_2O}\) is \(63.5 + 32 + 4 \times 16 + 5 \times 18 = 249.5\), of which the five waters of crystallisation contribute \(5 \times 18 = 90\). The percentage of water is therefore \(\dfrac{90}{249.5} \times 100 = 36.07\%\), i.e. **36 %**. 72 % is the intended trap, and it is a specific error rather than a random one: it is \(\dfrac{10 \times 18}{249.5} \times 100 = 72.1\%\), i.e. counting TEN waters of crystallisation instead of the five the formula actually carries. 10 % and 60 % follow from no consistent reading of the formula.

This is the subject of the chapter's section 2.8, *Use of graph in analysis*, whose opening sentence is that analytical chemistry "involves deducing some relation, if any, between two or more properties of matter under study" — and the method it then demonstrates, on volume against temperature, is **plotting a graph**: the points are plotted, an average curve is drawn through them, and the shape of that curve yields the relation \(V \propto T\). Mean deviation and relative error belong to section 2.3 and describe the scatter and the bias of ONE measured quantity; neither compares two properties, so neither can expose a relation between them. That also disposes of "all the above three".
